1553-64672026Oct19American journal of pharmaceutical educationAm J Pharm EducStudent facing assessment blueprint reduces assessment-related anxiety.10210910210910.1016/j.ajpe.2026.102109S0002-9459(26)01467-1To determine the effect of a student facing assessment blueprint on student assessment-related anxiety and the perceived value of the blueprint for students preparing for assessments in an Integrated Pharmacology and Therapeutics (IPT) unit within an undergraduate Pharmacy programme.Undergraduate pharmacy students completed the Westside Test Anxiety Scale following the IPT mid-semester test in two consecutive semesters in 2024 - in Semester 1, without assessment blueprints (baseline) and in Semester 2, when assessment blueprints were provided for the mid-semester test and final written examination. Anxiety Scale scores at the two time points were compared and students were invited to participate in a focus group discussion (FGD) following the final written examination in Semester 2.Fifty-eight and 53 students completed the Anxiety Scale in Semesters 1 and 2, respectively. The mean anxiety score was reduced from 3.71 in Semester 1 to 3.37 in Semester 2. Eight students participated in the FGD. Thematic analysis identified a perceived reduction in assessment-related anxiety attributed to enhanced focus and efficiency in preparing for assessments. Additionally, participants described the broader applicability of assessment blueprints to other units with high cognitive load.The student facing assessment blueprint reduces assessment-related anxiety and can be used as a valuable tool to support preparation for assessment within an IPT unit.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. 1178-2013212026International journal of nanomedicineInt J NanomedicineThymoquinone-Loaded Hexosomal Nanoparticles Attenuate Neuroinflammation and Improve Cognitive Function in an Alzheimer's Disease Mouse Model.62769262769262769210.2147/IJN.S627692Alzheimer's disease (AD) involves neuroinflammation that worsens cognitive decline. Thymoquinone (TQ) has potent anti-inflammatory activity, but its therapeutic application is limited by poor solubility, stability, and systemic bioavailability, which may restrict effective brain exposure. This study developed TQ-loaded hexosomal nanoparticles (TQ-HNP) to enhance TQ delivery and therapeutic efficacy in a dizocilpine (MK-801)- induced mouse model of AD.TQ-HNP were prepared using glyceryl monooleate, oleic acid, and poloxamer 407, optimized to ~104 nm size, -31 mV zeta potential, and ~95% entrapment efficiency. Following intraperitoneal administration of free TQ and TQ-HNP, male C57BL/6 mice treated with dizocilpine received intraperitoneal injections of free TQ or TQ-HNP and were subsequently evaluated for cognitive function (Novel Object Recognition test), anxiety-like behavior (Open Field test), and brain levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β.Dizocilpine impaired memory and increased anxiety-like behavior in assessed mice, while TQ-HNP significantly improved both outcomes compared to free TQ. TQ-HNP also reduced IL-6 in the hippocampus and cerebellum and lowered TNF-α and IL-1β in the cerebellum, confirming its anti-inflammatory efficacy.TQ-HNP enhanced the brain delivery of thymoquinone, mitigated neuroinflammation, and restored cognitive function in the AD-like mouse model, supporting its potential as a nanocarrier-based therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders.© 2026 Eissa et al.EissaNerminNDepartment of Biomedical Sciences, College of Health Sciences, Abu Dhabi University, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.AlwattarJana KJKDepartment of Pharmaceutical Sciences, School of Pharmacy, Lebanese International University, Beirut, Lebanon.JayaprakashPetrillaP0000-0001-5433-6587Department of Pharmacology & Therapeutics, College of Medicine and Health Sciences, United Arab Emirates University, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates.Al AssalyHayaHDepartment of Biomedical Sciences, College of Health Sciences, Abu Dhabi University, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.KharnoubRouaRDepartment of Biomedical Sciences, College of Health Sciences, Abu Dhabi University, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.AltalebAya AbedAADepartment of Biomedical Sciences, College of Health Sciences, Abu Dhabi University, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.AtifKhaloudKDepartment of Biomedical Sciences, College of Health Sciences, Abu Dhabi University, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.RahalMohamadMDepartment of Pharmaceutical Sciences, School of Pharmacy, Lebanese International University, Beirut, Lebanon.SadekBassemB0000-0002-0320-1487Department of Pharmacology & Therapeutics, College of Medicine and Health Sciences, United Arab Emirates University, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates.engJournal Article20261014

1467-11072026Oct19Cardiology in the youngCardiol YoungPalpitations in children and adolescents in the emergency department: a state-of-the-art narrative review of arrhythmia risk, diagnostic strategy, and disposition.1101-1010.1017/S1047951126124494Palpitations are not an uncommon complaint in the paediatric emergency department, causing significant anxiety for families concerned about serious heart disease. However, most cases are benign, often stemming from normal physiological responses like fever or anxiety. Primary cardiac arrhythmias are rare in this clinical setting.The main challenge is identifying the few children with dangerous arrhythmias among the many benign cases. Fear of missing a life-threatening condition often leads to extensive, costly, and stressful investigations, even in low-risk patients, without significantly improving detection rates.This review aims to create a structured, risk-based framework for evaluating paediatric palpitations in the emergency department. The goal is to help clinicians efficiently distinguish benign from potentially life-threatening causes, thereby optimising resource use and reducing family anxiety.A thorough clinical history, physical exam, and a standard 12-lead electrocardiogram are the most effective evaluation tools. "Red-flag" features-such as palpitations with fainting (syncope), onset during exercise, or a family history of sudden cardiac death-successfully identify nearly all children with significant arrhythmias. Barring certain risk factors and any abnormalities on a 12 lead electrocardiogram, a dangerous cardiac condition is highly unlikely.A stratified approach is recommended. Low-risk children (no red-flag features, normal electrocardiogram) can be safely discharged with reassurance. High-risk patients require immediate, aggressive evaluation, including cardiology consultation and potential hospital admission. This strategy improves accuracy, is cost-effective, and enhances patient safety.AbouelmagdKhaledK0000-0003-3919-9873Cardiology Department, Al-Azhar University Damietta Faculty of Medicine, Egypt.OyedeleTemitomi JaneTJDepartment of Medicine and Surgery, Bowen University, Nigeria.BergerGabrielaGSt. George's University School of Medicine, Grenada.FakhiraldeenSarahSCollege of Medicine, University of Baghdad, Iraq.Mohamed Ahmed ElMitwalli AliHabibaHGeneral Medicine Practice Program, Batterjee Medical College, Saudi Arabia.HishmatNouranNDepartment of Physical Therapy, May University in Cairo, Egypt.SadaqatAtiqullahAFaculty of Medicine, Kateb University, Afghanistan.CarrLauren ALAPediatric Emergency Medicine Attending Physician, Resident Director, Department of Emergency Medicine, St Christopher's Hospital for Children, USA.AlsabriMohammedMDepartment of Emergency Medicine, Al-Thawara Modern General Hospital, Sanaa, Yemen.Pediatric Emergency Department, Department of Pediatrics, St Christopher's Hospital for Children, USA.https://ror.org/05t3ett24engJournal ArticleReview20261019

1477-22052026Oct18Anxiety, stress, and copingAnxiety Stress CopingThe gender gap in math anxiety (and in the link between math anxiety and math achievement) is not so salient when other anxieties are controlled for.1221-2210.1080/10615806.2026.2745773Math anxiety (MA) is considered to affect math achievement and the choice of math-related educational paths, thus contributing to the gender gap in STEM careers. However, despite decades of research, the mechanisms underlying the relationships between gender, MA, and math achievement remain largely unclear. One of the reasons is that different types of anxiety and math achievement levels are rarely controlled for.We tested the associations between gender, MA, spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement in a sample of 269 adults.We replicated previous findings that spatial anxiety in areas of navigation and mental manipulation, but not imagery, mediates the relationship between gender and MA. Importantly, in light of previous contradictory findings, we found that math achievement significantly mediated this relationship. Crucially, we found that gender, spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement together accounted for 66% of the variance in MA, with gender uniquely accounting for only 5%.The commonly reported gender gap in MA is less pronounced when other anxieties are controlled for, especially given that we did not observe gender differences in the strength of the relationship between MA and math achievement.SzczygiełMonikaM0000-0001-6544-0734Institute of Psychology, Faculty of Philosophy, Jagiellonian University in Krakow, Krakow, Poland.HoholMateuszM0000-0003-0422-5488Mathematical Cognition and Learning Lab, Copernicus Center for Interdisciplinary Studies, Jagiellonian University in Krakow, Krakow, Poland.engJournal Article20261018

1869-41011712026Oct16Insights into imagingInsights ImagingPatient acceptance and experience with contrast-enhanced mammography in women with a personal history of breast cancer: findings from the COMBO trial.26210.1186/s13244-026-02434-xTo evaluate patient acceptance, tolerability and experience with contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) in women with a personal history of breast cancer undergoing routine post-surgical surveillance.This prospective cohort study, conducted within the COMBO Trial, included consecutive women with a personal history of breast cancer undergoing CEM instead of digital mammography (DM) for routine surveillance from January 2023 to February 2025. Immediately after the examination, participants completed an anonymous 16-question questionnaire assessing discomfort, pain, exam duration, pre-examination reassurance, information received, anxiety, contrast injection, satisfaction and comparative experience with prior DM. Responses used Likert-type scales. Descriptive and non-parametric analyses were performed (p < 0.05 statistically significant).Of 969 eligible women, 936 (mean age 58.2 years, SD ± 10.2 years) completed the questionnaire. CEM was perceived as comparable to prior DM in terms of discomfort (631/936; 67.4%), pain (725/936; 77.4%), positioning (717/936; 76.6%) and duration (601/936; 64.3%). Overall satisfaction was high (900/936; 96.2%), and 932/936 (99.6%) of participants would recommend CEM. Although 433/936 (46.3%) of women reported moderate-to-high pre-examination anxiety, higher anxiety was significantly associated with greater perceived discomfort, pain, uncomfortable positioning, longer examination duration, lower reassurance, lower comfort during contrast medium administration, and lower overall satisfaction (all p < 0.001).In this large cohort of breast cancer survivors, CEM demonstrated high acceptance, satisfaction and tolerability in post-surgical follow-up. Although pre-examination anxiety negatively influenced examination experience, it did not reduce patients' willingness to undergo CEM, supporting its integration into personalised post-treatment breast cancer surveillance.Question Evidence on patient acceptance and tolerability of CEM for routine post-surgical surveillance in women with previous breast cancer is limited. Findings In 936 breast cancer survivors, CEM showed high satisfaction and tolerability, while pre-examination anxiety was associated with a less favourable experience. Critical Relevance Statement High patient acceptance supports CEM as a feasible surveillance option after breast cancer treatment, while the association between anxiety and poorer experience highlights the radiologist's role in pre-examination communication and reassurance.© 2026. 1469-898663102026OctPsychophysiologyPsychophysiologyMathematics Anxiety Is Associated With Attentional and Memory-Related Neural Activity During Numerical Cognition.e70422e70422e7042210.1111/psyp.70422Mathematics achievement can be influenced by negative emotions and expectations related to numerical tasks. Individuals with high mathematics anxiety often show poorer numerical performance. This study investigated the neural mechanisms underlying different levels of numerical processing associated with mathematics anxiety using number line estimation and arithmetic verification tasks during fMRI. Participants were classified into high (n = 22, age = 23.09 ± 2.22) and low (n = 24, age = 22.67 ± 3.29) mathematics anxiety groups based on detailed screening prior to scanning. Trait and test anxiety were also assessed to capture broader anxiety-related characteristics. Before the fMRI session, participants completed assessments of calculation performance and digit span, and a mock MRI session was used to reduce scanner-related stress. Participants completed task and control conditions for each numerical task during fMRI. Neuroimaging data were analyzed using 2 × 2 whole-brain voxel-wise ANOVA. Group differences in task-related brain activation were further examined both before and after statistically controlling for trait and test anxiety. Results showed that low mathematics anxiety was associated with greater frontal eye field activity during number-space mapping and stronger supramarginal gyrus activity during arithmetic computation compared with high mathematics anxiety. Controlling for trait and test anxiety helped clarify which neural effects remained associated with mathematics anxiety after accounting for variance shared with broader anxiety-related factors. Overall, attentional and memory-related effects remained associated with mathematics anxiety after this adjustment, whereas additional effects involving motor processes and cognitive control were attenuated, suggesting that these effects may partly reflect variance shared with broader anxiety-related constructs.© 2026 The Author(s).
